extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travelogue / readers interested in comic performance and boating etiquette
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted prescriptive observations from a humorous travelogue about (a) what counts as suitable boating dress and picnic behaviour, and (b) practical and performative criteria for comic singing and entertaining an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boating costume for women
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'boating costume' ought to be a costume that can be worn in a boat, and not merely under a glass-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance and examples: avoid delicate, photographic-studio/French fashion-plate dresses that are ruined by spray or contact with grass; dresses should permit getting in/out of boats, tolerating a little water or dirt, and not distract wearers from enjoying the trip. Anti-pattern: ladies who fuss about the boat being 'not clean', sit bolt upright to avoid contact, shrink at every splash and thus spoil the excursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men's boating dress — show tasteful colours
rubrics_metrics.description: The river affords a good opportunity for dress; men are able to show their taste in colours (example preference: red and black, light-blue necktie, Russian-leather shoes, red silk handkerchief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical suggestion: choose colour combinations that flatter complexion (warning that bright yellows/oranges may not suit darker complexions). Avoid 'loud' apparel (e.g., a conspicuous blazer) if you don't want to attract attention to the boat. The narrator gives concrete stylistic prescriptions and an anti-pattern (Harris's ill-advised yellow/orange and George's loud blazer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oarsmanship etiquette to avoid splashing delicate passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: When sculling with passengers in fragile dress, an oarsman should feather some two feet high, pause at the end of each stroke to let the blades drip before returning them, and pick a smooth bit of water to drop them into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical technique: steady, careful rowing reduces spray; if necessary change places (row bow instead of stroke) to limit splashing. Anti-pattern: rollicking, dashing strokes that send spray over passengers and relieve them of discomfort (Bow's behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boating-picnic participation — chores as part of the fun
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in simple picnic tasks (e.g., washing up) is part of the enjoyment and should be encouraged, even for guests who appear unpractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: gently instruct novices how to 'tuck 'em up' and sloush dishes in the water; turning what looks like menial work into shared amusement can relieve social stiffness. Anti-pattern: expecting some guests to remain aloof from basic picnic chores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper tourist behaviour in villages (churchyards norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is presented as the proper thing, when you get to a village or town, to rush off to the churchyard and enjoy the graves and read epitaphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as a social norm of the narrator's milieu (though the narrator himself playfully refuses it). Guidance here is cultural rather than technical: visiting local churchyards and inscriptions is counted as the expected pastime for travellers in these parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to respond to riverside blackmail/trespass demands
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper course when accosted by someone claiming you are trespassing is to offer your name and address and leave the matter to the owner to summon you and prove any damage rather than yielding to on-the-spot demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: do not pay or give in to riverside roughs who demand money as if on the proprietor's behalf; the majority pay because they are lazy or timid. If the riparian proprietor truly has a claim, let them take the formal step of summoning and proving damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation for comic song performance — what matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In a comic song one may not need a fine voice, strict phrasing, or perfect rhythm, but one does expect the performer to know and deliver the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience tolerance: minor vocal faults and timing slips are acceptable, but forgetting lyrics or failing to deliver the textual content ruins the effect. Example guidance: words and intelligible narrative/lines are essential; absence of these is the main fault (see Harris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns in comic singing (what not to do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors that destroy a comic-song performance include: remembering only the first three lines and repeating them; breaking off mid-line and sniggering; attempting to improvise nonsensical lines; mixing up different songs; failing to coordinate with the accompanist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples from Harris: repeatedly cycling through the opening lines, interrupting for asides, confusing songs (mixing Judge's song, Admiral's song, etc.), causing accompanist confusion and audience discomfort. These are explicit anti-patterns to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan/earnest manner as a comic technique (and its risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: An intensely serious, almost pathetic delivery can make a song irresistibly amusing — the performer's gravity creates a comic contrast with the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Herr Slossenn Boschen's solemn delivery of a song (whose words were actually tragic) produced uncontrollable laughter; the seriousness amplified comic perception. Caution: this technique can backfire — the performer may be genuinely offended if the audience laughs at material the performer intended sincerely (the Professor reacted angrily).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match entertainment to audience and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Select acts and amusements suited to the class, tastes, and cultural understanding of the company gathered; introducing material beyond the audience's frame (or out of place) risks misunderstanding or offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: two students brought a German Professor to sing what they touted as a comic song; the cultured party misread the performance, laughed, and the Professor felt insulted. Moral: know your audience and cultural codes before arranging novelty acts.
